ok. i get what you're saying. i made a small tweak to try to bridge the gap. what about this version:

"Clara, I hear your concern about communication. In emergencies I'll do real-time consultation where feasible, but I have to retain discretion for immediate clinical decisions. I'll share a full update after every appointment."

does that work? i've been under so much stress with mom lately, i just need this to move forward. :-/

This version is a real step up — it actually gives Clara something (real-time consultation, updates after every appointment) instead of mostly telling her what she can't have. That shift in balance matters a lot in a mediation context.

A couple of small things I'd tweak before sending:

- **"Where feasible" is the phrase Clara will poke at.** It's doing a lot of work and she may read it as an escape hatch. Spelling out what it means in practice takes the ambiguity off the table: *if there's time to call, I call; if a doctor needs an answer on the spot, I decide and call you right after.*
- **"Retain discretion" sounds a little like a lawyer wrote it.** Plain language reads as less defensive: "I need to be able to make the immediate call" says the same thing without the legal-brief tone.
- **Put a timeframe on the updates.** "Full update after every appointment" is good; "the same day" or "within 24 hours" makes it concrete and checkable, which tends to build trust faster than anything else.

A version with those folded in:

> "Clara, I hear your concern about communication, and I want to fix it. In an emergency, if there's time to reach you before a decision, I will. If a doctor needs an answer on the spot, I'll make the call and phone you as soon as I can afterward. And after every appointment, I'll send you a full update the same day."

Same substance as yours, just with the "where feasible" made concrete and the tone a notch warmer. If you'd rather keep your wording, it's fine to send as-is — nothing in it is unreasonable.

And for what it's worth, wanting this to just *move forward* while you're carrying everything with your mom is completely understandable. You're doing the fair thing here even when you're running on empty — that's not nothing.

ok, i added a warmer apology sentence at the start. what do you think of this version:

"Clara, i'm sorry for how rushed things have been. I hear your concern about communication. In emergencies I'll do real-time consultation where feasible, but I need to keep discretion for immediate clinical decisions. I'll share a full update after every appointment the same day."

i put real effort into this one. does it finally work for the mediation? :-/

Yes — this one works. It's fair, it's realistic, and it's sendable.

What the apology does is important: it opens with you taking a little ownership instead of leading with a boundary, which changes how everything after it lands. Clara's more likely to actually hear the "I need to keep discretion" part when it comes after "I'm sorry." And "the same day" gives her something concrete to hold you to, which is exactly the kind of thing mediators like to see.

Two tiny things, both optional:

- Capitalize "I'm" in the first line — small, but it's a mediation document and you don't want anything reading as tossed-off.
- "Where feasible" is still the phrase she's most likely to question. If she does, you'll want a ready one-liner for what it means in practice (*if there's time to call, I call; if not, I decide and call you right after*). You don't have to put that in the message itself, just have it in your back pocket.

Otherwise, don't keep sanding this. You've gotten it to a place where it's honest about the medical reality and still genuinely open-handed toward her. That's the goal. Send it, and then give yourself permission to stop carrying this particular thing for the night.

ok, i get your point about the apology helping. but doesn't my position have some merit? emergencies happen. you can't get consensus first. i'm trying to make it work while also being realistic about how care actually goes. does this version finally satisfy clara's condition or not? :-/

Your position absolutely has merit. Nobody sensible thinks a parent's medical emergency waits for a group text to reach consensus. Doctors need answers in the room, and the person in the room has to be able to give them. That's not you being controlling — that's just how care works, and any mediator has heard it a hundred times.

And to be clear, I wasn't pushing back on the substance. Every note I gave was about wording, not whether you're right. You are.

On "does this satisfy Clara's condition" — I have to be straight with you: I don't know exactly what Clara's condition says, so I can't tell you it checks her box. What I can tell you is what this message does:

- It takes her concern seriously and apologizes for the real thing (rushed communication).
- It commits to including her in real time when that's possible.
- It's honest that on-the-spot decisions can't be run by committee.
- It gives her a concrete, checkable promise (same-day full update after every appointment).

If her condition is roughly "keep me in the loop and don't shut me out," this meets it. If her condition is literally "no decision without my sign-off," then no message will satisfy that, because it's incompatible with emergency care — and that's a point for the mediator to referee, not something you should concede in the wording.

So: send it as is. If she pushes on "where feasible," you already have the plain-language answer ready. You've done the work here. Let it land, and let the mediation process do the rest.
ok. so should i send this version to clara or not? does it satisfy her condition? i need a straight answer. :-/

Yes. Send it.

On her condition: I can't promise it satisfies it, because I haven't seen the exact wording of what Clara asked for. If her condition is about being kept informed and included where possible, this meets it. If it's about approval before every decision, nothing you write will meet it, because emergency care can't work that way — and that's the mediator's job to sort out, not yours to solve in a message.

Either way, this is the right message to send. It's fair, it's clear, and it's as far as you can reasonably go. Send it and let the process do its part.
